summary:
Armenia decriminalised consensual same-sex conduct in 2003. There is no statute of the restrictive type operating in neighbouring Azerbaijan. In 2013 police proposed a bill criminalising "non-traditional sexual relationships" and LGBT "propaganda" directed at young people, modelled on Russian legislation; it failed to pass after Pink Armenia argued it functioned as a distraction tactic.

Same-sex marriage is prohibited. The legal framework offers trans visitors little affirmative protection: there is no discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and the anti-discrimination bill tabled in 2018 did not pass. Hate-crime protection covering bias-motivated violence has been characterised as ambiguous since 2022.

Legal gender recognition exists as an administrative practice and has been available since 2006, but it requires surgery. Gender-affirming care is restricted, and there is no legal recognition of non-binary gender.

Enforcement of law and order provides thin protection in practice. In May 2012 the gay-friendly DIY bar in Yerevan was firebombed with a Molotov cocktail by suspected neo-Nazis; police took twelve hours to respond, and two suspects were later detained through CCTV footage. In April 2019 Lilit Martirosyan, Armenia's first registered trans woman, became the first trans person to speak at the National Assembly, addressing LGBTI discrimination; she then received extensive death threats by Facebook and email, including from members of parliament who called for her to be burned alive. In February 2020 a member of a nationalist party burned incense over the same lectern, denouncing her speech as a desecration.

Official and private restriction of LGBT expression is recurrent. In 2017 organisers of the Yerevan International Film Festival cancelled the screening of two LGBT-themed films after negative public reaction. In November 2018 a Christian LGBT group was forced to cancel planned forums and events, citing constant threats and organised intimidation from political and religious leaders and what it described as insufficient police readiness to protect them. In 2014 the Iravunk newspaper published a list of dozens of Armenian LGBT Facebook accounts, describing them as "zombies"; the Court of Appeals ruled the newspaper had not offended anyone and ordered the plaintiffs to pay 50,000 dram (about US$120) to the newspaper.

Documented violence against LGBT people is severe and ongoing. Pink Armenia's 2024 annual report records discrimination, torture and inhuman or degrading treatment including sexual violence, domestic violence and extortion, violations of private and family life, discrimination in education and work, and hate speech, including a chapter on pressure directed at a transgender individual who participated in a beauty pageant. The 2009 ILGA-Europe and COC fact-finding report "Forced Out: LGBT People in Armenia" documented societal and institutional homophobia, harassment, violence and discrimination in education, work and services.

Public acceptance is very low: Equaldex scores Armenia at 5 out of 100, and a 2012 study found 55% of Armenians would end a relationship with a friend or relative who came out, while 70% described LGBT people as "strange".
tangentialFactors:
Neighbouring Azerbaijan retains a criminal statute of the restrictive type that Armenia abolished in 2003; regional legal frameworks vary sharply, and visitors crossing the border should not assume Armenian conditions apply.

Hate-crime protection covering bias-motivated violence has been described as ambiguous since 2022, meaning the statutory basis for charging bias-motivated attacks is uncertain rather than clearly absent.

Restrictions on gender-affirming care and the surgical prerequisite for legal gender change are administrative and medical in character rather than criminal; they affect documents and treatment access rather than lawful presence in the country.

Recorded incidents of anti-LGBT violence include a 2012 arson attack on a gay-friendly bar in Yerevan in which police response took twelve hours, and death threats against the country's first trans parliamentary speaker in 2019, some from sitting members of parliament. Both indicate a gap between formal legality and protective enforcement.

The 2009 "Forced Out" mission report remains a reference point for institutional homophobia in policing, education and health services, but predates decriminalisation's downstream effects and the subsequent period of activist organising.
localsOnly:
Legal gender recognition has been available as an administrative procedure since 2006, on condition of surgical intervention. Residents seeking marker changes must meet that requirement, and non-binary recognition is not available.

Gender-affirming care is restricted for residents as well as visitors, with treatment pathways constrained by medical regulation.

The anti-discrimination bill tabled in 2018 did not pass, so residents have no statutory claim on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity in employment, education, housing or services. Cases of discrimination in education and work are documented in Pink Armenia's reporting but are pursued, where at all, outside a dedicated protection statute.

Pink Armenia's 2024 report documents domestic violence and extortion affecting LGBT residents, alongside torture and inhuman or degrading treatment including sexual violence, and violations of private and family life. The organisation also recorded hate speech and targeted pressure on a transgender individual over participation in a beauty pageant.

Community organising has faced organised intimidation. In November 2018 a Christian LGBT group cancelled forums and events after threats from political and religious leaders, citing what it described as insufficient police readiness to protect participants.

A 2012 study found 55% of Armenians would end a relationship with a friend or relative who came out, and 70% found LGBT people "strange"; Equaldex records a public-opinion acceptance score of 5 out of 100. Coming out therefore carries substantial social and family cost.
outOfScopeNotes:
Hate-crime protection is characterised as "ambiguous" rather than absent or present; the underlying statutory wording and prosecutorial practice are not resolved in the sources consulted here.

The scope of restrictions on gender-affirming care is not specified in the sources: which treatments are restricted, by which regulation, and under what conditions is unresolved.

The 2024 findings in Pink Armenia's report are presented as documented allegations and organisational reporting; individual case outcomes, prosecutions and court dispositions are not sourced here.

The February 2020 incense-burning incident at the National Assembly lectern is described in reporting as a denunciation by a nationalist party member; any criminal or disciplinary follow-up is not sourced here.

No source in the current inventory addresses entry, visa or border screening questions for trans visitors, including how gender markers on passports are treated by Armenian border authorities. That layer of the assessment is not sourced.
